texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Q: I work at a big company and my team and I keep trying to launch a “big bet” project (one with a lot of upside but that’ll take a while to build), and our resources keep getting pulled away. Any advice for maintaining support for a big bet?
texts.text: Q: I work at a big company and my team and I keep trying to launch a “big bet” project (one with a lot of upside but that’ll take a while to build), and our resources keep getting pulled away. Any advice for maintaining support for a big bet?

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I like to think of a “big bet” project like a highly-experimental new weapon that you’re trying to smuggle to the front. There are forces at play that want this project squashed, and if you charge ahead without the proper support or make any missteps, you’ll get discovered and taken out.
texts.text: I like to think of a “big bet” project like a highly-experimental new weapon that you’re trying to smuggle to the front. There are forces at play that want this project squashed, and if you charge ahead without the proper support or make any missteps, you’ll get discovered and taken out.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You do this by consistently shipping small but consistent wins: moving your KPIs, hitting goals, and showing progress. With this cover in place, you’ll be able to smuggle the big bet through and emerge on the other side with a game-changing new product.
texts.text: You do this by consistently shipping small but consistent wins: moving your KPIs, hitting goals, and showing progress. With this cover in place, you’ll be able to smuggle the big bet through and emerge on the other side with a game-changing new product.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I’ve done this time and again, and I’ve found this strategy to be the only way to consistently maintain the buy-in and resources necessary to work on a long-term project at larger companies, on most teams.
texts.text: I’ve done this time and again, and I’ve found this strategy to be the only way to consistently maintain the buy-in and resources necessary to work on a long-term project at larger companies, on most teams.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Tactically, my rule of thumb is to spend 80% of my team’s time on short-term low-risk incremental wins, and 20% on high-risk, long-term bets. This way, we can continue to move our KPIs while bringing our big bet alongside. Here’s how that might look on a roadmap:

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Even you do have the trust and cover of the current leaders, people and priorities change. When there are new fires, people will come looking for non-essential projects in progress to pull resources from. If your project hasn’t shown any concrete benefits for a while, and the upside is uncertain, it’ll be easy picking.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Note: This advice applies mostly to larger companies, and to the average team. Some teams are top-down designated to work on long-term high-risk projects, in which case this is less likely to be an issue. Similarly, at early-stage startups, most everything you work on is a high-risk long-term big bet. If this isn’t an issue for you, don’t sweat it.
